Gleipnir 1.1.0 -- usage reference
============================

Run `gleipnir --help` for a short version of the option list below.


COMMANDS
--------

  gleipnir c [opts] archive path...              compress files or directories
  gleipnir x [opts] archive [dir] [member...]    extract
  gleipnir t [opts] archive                      check integrity
  gleipnir l [opts] archive                      list contents
  gleipnir r archive out.gl                     rebuild damaged segments

`x`, `e` and `d` all extract and are interchangeable. Note that 7-Zip's `e`
flattens directories and Gleipnir's does not. Gleipnir always restores the stored
structure, so here `e` and `x` are the same thing.

If you extract with no directory given, files land in the current directory.
Naming specific members after the directory extracts only those:

  gleipnir x archive.gl restored a.txt logs/x.log

Exit codes, which are the contract for scripting:

  0    success, and for `t`, the archive verified
  1    usage or I/O error: bad flag, missing path, unreadable file, full disk
  2    archive corrupt, or verification failed

1 and 2 are deliberately different. A scheduled check needs to distinguish
"the disk is rotting" from "the path was wrong", because those page different
people.


OPTIONS
-------

  -1 .. -9    preset, -1 fastest .. -9 smallest (default -5)
              Only six are distinct: -4, -6 and -8 are aliases for -3, -5
              and -7 in this release.
  -f1, -f2    throughput presets, below -1 on cost.  -f2 is smaller and
              slower than -1, so the real cost order is:
                  f1, 1, f2, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9
  -mN         resize every context table by 2^N.  -m-1 halves them, -m1
              doubles them.  Lower means less memory and slightly worse
              ratio.
  -tN         worker threads.  -t0 means all cores.  Default 1.
  -sN         segment size in MB (default 64).  Smaller bounds memory and
              limits how much one damaged region costs you, and larger
              compresses slightly better.
  -w0         do not word-transform text.  By default a segment that is
              mostly words is dictionary-coded before modelling, which is
              smaller and faster on prose and markup.
  -pN         recovery records: one parity block per N segments.  `-p` alone
              means 32, costing about 3%.  Default off.
  -D          with `t`, decode everything and verify SHA-256 as well
  -L          with `l`, also print each member's SHA-256
  -M          with `l`, print a sha256sum-compatible manifest
  -x GLOB     exclude paths matching GLOB.  Repeatable.  Matched against
              both the stored name and the bare filename, so -x "*.log"
              works regardless of directory.
  -q          quiet
  --version   print version and archive format
  --help      print the option list


TYPICAL USE
-----------

Compress a folder, check it, extract it:

  gleipnir c archive.gl myfolder
  gleipnir t archive.gl
  gleipnir d archive.gl restored

For cold storage:

  gleipnir c -5 -t0 -p32 archive.gl /data
  gleipnir t archive.gl

then delete the originals yourself, once `gleipnir t` has passed. Gleipnir never
deletes or modifies anything you point it at.

Excluding things you do not want stored:

  gleipnir c archive.gl /data -x "*.tmp" -x "cache/*" -x "*.iso"

Saving an inventory next to the archive, so its contents are auditable
without opening it:

  gleipnir l -M archive.gl > archive.manifest

After restoring, that manifest can be checked with a tool that shares no
code with Gleipnir at all:

  sha256sum -c archive.manifest


CHOOSING A PRESET
-----------------

Measured on the Silesia corpus (211,938,580 bytes), single thread, all in
one session:

  preset   output       compress    decompress   RAM (compress)
  -f1      43.2 MB      1.91 MB/s   1.92 MB/s       203 MB
  -1       42.6 MB      1.67 MB/s   1.66 MB/s       195 MB
  -f2      40.9 MB      1.38 MB/s   1.38 MB/s       237 MB
  -2       40.3 MB      1.22 MB/s   1.21 MB/s       233 MB
  -3       39.4 MB      0.94 MB/s   0.93 MB/s       304 MB
  -5       38.0 MB      0.66 MB/s   0.65 MB/s       482 MB
  -7       36.4 MB      0.48 MB/s   0.48 MB/s       954 MB
  -9       35.5 MB      0.32 MB/s   0.32 MB/s      1193 MB

Every step up the ladder costs roughly 11-13x more time per 1% of size it
saves, from -2 upward. There is no bargain rung. Pick the slowest one you can
afford to wait for, twice, once now and once when you restore.

From -f1 to -5, decompression needs 37-39 MB MORE memory than compression.
The RAM column above is the compression figure, so size a restore machine
off the larger number. At -7 and -9 the two are within 10 MB.

Times vary between sessions -- -7's has moved by up to 22% -- so treat any
single figure as approximate. Sizes are exact.


VERIFYING WITHOUT A FULL RESTORE
--------------------------------

  gleipnir t archive.gl       checks stored checksums.  Runs at disk speed.
  gleipnir t -D archive.gl    decodes everything and checks SHA-256 per member.
                          Runs at compression speed, so ~1300x slower.

The fast check is what makes routine scrubbing affordable: on a 2.2 GB
archive it takes seconds where the deep check takes most of an hour. It
catches storage decay, meaning bits that changed on disk after writing, which
is the failure that actually happens to archived data.

Use `gleipnir t` on a schedule. Use `gleipnir t -D` before you rely on a restore.

A scheduled scrub is just:

  gleipnir t archive.gl || echo "archive failed check" | mail -s ALERT you@host


RECOVERY RECORDS
----------------

`-pN` writes one parity block per N segments: the XOR of every compressed
block in the group. Any ONE damaged segment per group can then be rebuilt
from the survivors.

  gleipnir c -p32 archive.gl /data     about 3% larger
  gleipnir t archive.gl                reports which segments are damaged
  gleipnir r archive.gl fixed.gl      writes a repaired copy

`r` never modifies the damaged archive. It writes a new one. A repaired
segment is fully decoded and checksummed before it is accepted, so a
"repair" that produced wrong bytes fails loudly instead of being written.

Two losses in the same group can't be recovered. If the data matters, keep a
second copy. Parity is not a backup.


MEMORY AND THREADS
------------------

Each worker thread holds a complete model, so memory is roughly

  (model size for the preset) x (thread count)

`-t8 -9` therefore wants about 8 GB. Gleipnir clamps the thread count to what the
machine can actually hold rather than thrashing, but a lower preset is
usually a better answer than being clamped.

`-sN` bounds the other half. A segment is loaded whole, so smaller segments
mean less peak memory and less lost to one damaged region, at a small cost
in ratio.


WHAT GLEIPNIR TOUCHES
----------------

Inputs are opened read-only. There is no delete call anywhere in the
program, so it can't remove your files.

The one thing Gleipnir overwrites without asking is its own output. If the
archive name given to `c` already exists it is replaced, and `d` overwrites
same-named files in the destination directory. Be careful with the
destination and not the source.

Extraction refuses unsafe member names, meaning absolute paths, drive letters
and anything containing "..", so a malicious archive cannot write outside the
directory you chose.


KNOWN LIMITS
------------

  * Decompression is as slow as compression, inherently. If you need fast
    restores, use zstd or xz instead.
  * No encryption. Encrypting an archive afterwards destroys the ability to
    scrub or repair it, since neither the checksums nor the parity blocks
    are readable through ciphertext.
  * No append. Adding to an archive means rewriting it.
  * No random access: a member is decoded from the start of its segments.
  * Archives are format v3; 1.1 reads v2 and v3, earlier builds read v2 only.
  * Verified to 2.2 GB per file. Nothing larger has been tried.
  * Recovery covers one lost segment per group and not two.
  * Tested on Windows and on Ubuntu 26.04. Other Linux distributions build
    from the same Makefile but haven't been tried.
